answer.answer:
Standardising the product range opens up seven things in the record, and they are not equally well supported. The strongest are industrialised production at scale, design for manufacture and assembly, and modular product architecture, with reduced construction complexity and a kit-of-parts configurator close behind, and robotic assembly relying on standardised components as its precondition; the weakest by a wide margin is the ability to accommodate late design changes, asserted in only a softened form and exhibited by 2 of the 50 coded cases. None of what follows is a machine: every downstream item is a design attribute, a process, an artefact or a value, so the payoff of standardisation is organisational and design-side rather than equipment. Note also that standardisation and modularity enable each other, so this is a loop rather than a one-way ladder, and there is no deployed project record in front of me here, only the coded case counts and the literature; "product range" and "becomes possible" are my paraphrase of what the record calls an attribute and its outbound enabling edges.

**What follows from AT7 "Highly standardised" (Attribute)**

AT7 is drawn on by 25 of the 50 coded cases [1] and carries 2 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges, all of which are listed in the context [1], so the set below is exact and may be read as the complete downstream picture.

Reading each relation for its logical direction rather than its arrow direction, standardisation is upstream of seven things:

- **Industrialised production (AT8, Attribute).** Industrialised depends on Highly standardised: industrialised-construction scale depends on standardisation [2], backed by peer-reviewed evidence, and the edge is carried by 16 of the 50 coded cases [1], the highest of any edge touching AT7. AT8 itself is drawn on by 23 of the 50 cases [1].
- **DfMA for DFAB process (PR9, Process).** Highly standardised enables DfMA for DFAB process: design standardisation and simplification is a DfMA enabler for offsite construction (peer-reviewed; carried by 13 of the 50 coded cases) [1]. PR9 is drawn on by 15 of the 50 cases [1].
- **Reduce construction complexity (VA7, Value).** Highly standardised enables Reduce construction complexity, on the mechanism that the base module standard reduces component variety and coordinates design, manufacture and assembly, on standard evidence [3], carried by 15 of the 50 coded cases [1]; VA7 is drawn on by 16 of the 50 [1].
- **Modular (AT2, Attribute).** Highly standardised enables Modular: decoupled standardised interfaces enable modular architecture and component interchange, peer-reviewed [4], carried by 11 of the 50 coded cases [1]; AT2 is drawn on by 12 of the 50 [1].
- **Configurators/kit-of-parts (AR6, Artefact).** Highly standardised enables Configurators/kit-of-parts, on the mechanism that modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components, on standard evidence [5], carried by 11 of the 50 coded cases [1]; AR6 is drawn on by 12 of the 50 [1].
- **Robotic assembly (PR4, Process).** Highly standardised enables Robotic assembly, on the finding that Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components (peer-reviewed; carried by 10 of the 50 coded cases) [1]. PR4 is drawn on by 13 of the 50 [1].
- **Accommodate late design changes (VA21, Value).** Highly standardised enables Accommodate late design changes, on the ground that standardisation of interfaces supports interchangeability and system flexibility, with the note that this is a terminological review and the claim was softened [6]; the edge is carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases [1] and VA21 is drawn on by only 3 of the 50 [1]. This is the one promise in the set that the coded record barely supports.

**The loop back into standardisation**

Standardisation is not purely a starting point. Modular enables Highly standardised, because modular architecture reduces the variety of component sizes produced [7], an edge carried by 11 of the 50 coded cases [1]. Together with DEP53 in the opposite direction this is a mutually reinforcing pair, not a linear sequence, so a programme can enter it from either the interface-standard side or the modular-architecture side.

**Second-order consequences**

The near neighbours extend the reach, though these are one hop further out: Configurators/kit-of-parts enables Mass-customisation, where the design configurator integrates customisation data into robotic manufacturing (peer-reviewed; carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases) [1]; Modular enables DfMA for DFAB process through alignment of product and process modularity (carried by 7 of the 50) [1]; and Industrialised enables Improve quality/performance, on evidence from Japanese housemakers that quality-oriented industrialised production considerably increases housing quality by providing standard fittings, carried by 22 of the 50 coded cases [1].

**What to watch**

Industrialised scale is not free once you have the standard: Industrialised depends on Delivery/business model/work culture, since adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models (carried by 13 of the 50 coded cases) [1]. Working the other way, Bespoke/customised design constrains Modular, because integral architecture couples functions tightly to components (carried by 4 of the 50) [1], so bespoke work erodes the modularity that feeds standardisation. And the standardisation route carries its own downside enabler in the coded record: Design compromise/over standardised is drawn on by 17 of the 50 coded cases [1], though the context gives it no dependency edges to place it against AT7.

**Phase and evidence limits**

AT7 applies in the Design phase, spans all phases, and its phase role is neutral [8]. The context carries no deployed process record, census record or named firm for any of these edges, so this answer rests on the coded case counts and the cited literature and standards, not on a specific project. The co-occurrence links from AT7 shown here are a statistical cut and assert no direction, so they should not be read as further consequences of standardising.
